initial_observation.encounter_context: presented with a one-month history of abdominal pain, admitted for diagnostic workup
initial_observation.chief_complaint: one-month history of dull abdominal pain localized in the left hypochondriac region
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The patient had a history of Child's B liver cirrhosis and portal hypertension, with splenomegaly and low WBC and platelet counts. Vital signs were normal and no fever was present. Abdominal exam showed Hackett's Grade 2 splenomegaly without stigmata of chronic liver disease
presenting_symptoms: one-month history of dull left hypochondriac abdominal pain
known_prior_history: low platelet counts of 54 x 10^9 cells/L

evidence_items.source_text: Upon admission, a contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen was scheduled, revealing a saccular-type SAA at the mid to distal splenic artery measuring 3.4 x 3.4 x 4.3 cm (AP x W x CC) with thrombus and splenic infarction as depicted in Figures 1-2.

A decision was made to perform angiographic coiling of the SAA. The femoral artery on the right side was punctured to establish vascular access for embolization. Following the identification of the SAA, fibered angiocoils of different sizes along with 2 ml of lipiodol were utilised as the embolisation material. Lipiodol, an iodine-based embolisation material, helped to delineate the vessel architecture better. The procedure was considered successful upon visual confirmation of thrombosis within the SAA.

A follow-up CT angiogram was conducted to assess the splenic artery post-coiling. The imaging revealed a thrombosed splenic artery, evident from the opacification of the splenic artery branch, as illustrated in Figure 3.

During a follow-up visit to the vascular clinic, there was a notable improvement in the patient's blood counts. The follow-up peripheral blood parameters indicated an increase in WBC from 1.9 to 5.0 x 10^9 cells/L and platelet counts from 54 to 209 x 10^9 cells/L.
Another follow-up CT of the abdomen demonstrated a reduction in spleen size from 10.8 x 7.4 x 18.6 to 9.3 x 5.4 x 16.1 cm (AP x W x CC), as shown in Figure 4.
In this case report, we present the instance of a woman with SAA and hypersplenism who initially complained of vague left-sided abdominal pain, coinciding with underlying Child's B liver cirrhosis.

As stated, relevant blood counts indicate leucopaenia and thrombocytopaenia consistent with hypersplenism.
